column1: # BacFlux trait rules, version 1 (hand-curated): one row per trait, called from sets of genes defined in trait_genes_v1.tsv. The columns and how a call is made are explained in docs/analysis/traits.md.

column8: caveat
column9: assay

column5: vnfD | vnfG | vnfK | anfD | anfG | anfK
column8: A call means the nitrogenase and FeMo-cofactor genes are present, not that the strain fixes N2 in culture or in soil: nitrogenase is switched off by ammonium and destroyed by oxygen, and many rhizobia fix N2 only inside root nodules.
column9: Acetylene reduction to ethylene, measured by gas chromatography, in cells grown in nitrogen-free medium at low oxygen (Hardy et al. 1968, doi:10.1104/pp.43.8.1185).

column8: Nod genes show that the strain can make Nod factors, not that it nodulates or fixes nitrogen with a given legume, and some photosynthetic bradyrhizobia nodulate without them.
column9: Nodulation test on the host legume in sterile culture (Somasegaran & Hoben 1994, doi:10.1007/978-1-4613-8375-8)
column10: Dénarié et al. 1996, doi:10.1146/annurev.bi.65.070196.002443; John et al. 1993, doi:10.1073/pnas.90.2.625; Atkinson & Long 1992, doi:10.1094/MPMI-5-439; Giraud et al. 2007, doi:10.1126/science.1139548

column8: A call does not prove an active enzyme (nickel and, in most bacteria, the UreD/E/F/G accessory proteins are also needed) or a plant benefit (fast urea hydrolysis can lose nitrogen as ammonia), and urease genes are so widespread that a call says little to rank strains.
column9: Christensen urea agar (Christensen 1946, doi:10.1128/jb.52.4.461-466.1946); urease activity raises the pH, which turns the phenol red indicator pink.

column2: Mineral phosphate solubilisation (gluconic acid via PQQ glucose dehydrogenase)
column8: A call does not measure how much phosphate the strain dissolves, which depends on glucose supply and soil buffering, and strains without the call may still solubilise phosphate with other organic acids.
column9: Phosphate released from tricalcium phosphate in NBRIP broth, measured colorimetrically; the halo on NBRIP or Pikovskaya agar is a quick screen but misses some solubilisers (Nautiyal 1999, doi:10.1111/j.1574-6968.1999.tb13383.x).

column8: A phytase gene does not guarantee phytate use in soil, where most phytate is bound to minerals; histidine acid phytases work best at acid pH and beta-propeller phytases need calcium and neutral pH.
column9: Clearing halo on calcium- or sodium-phytate agar, confirmed by the two-step counterstain that rules out acid production (Bae et al. 1999, doi:10.1016/S0167-7012(99)00096-2), then phosphate release from phytate in a liquid assay.

column4: phoA | phoD | phoX | pafA | aphA | phoN
column8: Most bacteria carry at least one of these phosphatases and, except PafA, make them only when phosphate is scarce, so a call says little to rank strains.
column9: p-Nitrophenyl phosphate hydrolysis (Tabatabai & Bremner 1969, doi:10.1016/0038-0717(69)90012-1) by cells grown in low-phosphate medium, which induces the alkaline phosphatases, although PafA is made whether phosphate is scarce or not (Torriani 1960, doi:10.1016/0006-3002(60)91281-6; Lidbury et al. 2022, doi:10.1073/pnas.2118122119).
column10: Lidbury et al. 2022, doi:10.1073/pnas.2118122119; Ragot et al. 2015, doi:10.1128/AEM.01823-15; Sebastian & Ammerman 2009, doi:10.1038/ismej.2009.10; Rossolini et al. 1998, doi:10.1007/s000180050212

column8: A complete C-P lyase lets a strain use phosphonates as a phosphorus source when phosphate is scarce; it does not mean the strain degrades glyphosate, which only some C-P lyase carriers can do.
column9: Growth with methylphosphonate (or 2-aminoethylphosphonate) as the only phosphorus source in phosphate-free medium (Metcalf & Wanner 1991, doi:10.1128/jb.173.2.587-600.1991).
column10: Metcalf & Wanner 1993, doi:10.1128/jb.175.11.3430-3442.1993; Jochimsen et al. 2011, doi:10.1073/pnas.1104922108; Kamat et al. 2011, doi:10.1038/nature10622; Hove-Jensen et al. 2014, doi:10.1128/MMBR.00040-13

column8: A call means the genes for a pyoverdine are present; it does not say which of the many pyoverdine side chains the strain makes, nor how much iron it frees in a real soil.
column9: CAS agar for siderophore activity (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9), and pyoverdine itself as a yellow-green, water-soluble pigment that fluoresces under UV (Meyer & Abdallah 1978, doi:10.1099/00221287-107-2-319; Meyer 2000, doi:10.1007/s002030000188); an iron-poor medium such as King's B is the usual choice.

column8: A call means the strain can assemble the catecholate enterobactin, not that it also decorates it with glucose to make salmochelin, which needs iroB.
column9: CAS agar, or the CAS overlay on colonies grown on any solid medium (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9; Perez-Miranda et al. 2007, doi:10.1016/j.mimet.2007.03.023).

column8: A call means the bacillibactin cluster is present, and because bacillibactin shares its catechol head group with enterobactin and vibriobactin, a positive CAS plate on its own cannot tell these three apart.
column9: CAS agar, or the CAS overlay on colonies (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9; Perez-Miranda et al. 2007, doi:10.1016/j.mimet.2007.03.023).

column8: A call means a desferrioxamine-type hydroxamate cluster is present; it does not say which desferrioxamine (B, E or G) is made, and it does not separate it from the closely related bisucaberin and putrebactin clusters, which are built by the same four enzyme families.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); hydroxamate siderophores also give a positive Csaky-type test, as used to measure the N-hydroxylation step of this pathway (Giddings et al. 2021, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0248385), and the particular desferrioxamine is identified by HPLC-MS.
column10: Barona-Gomez et al. 2004, doi:10.1021/ja045774k; Challis 2005, doi:10.1002/cbic.200400283; Giddings et al. 2021, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0248385; Salomone-Stagni et al. 2018, doi:10.1016/j.jsb.2018.02.002

column8: A call cannot say whether the strain makes pyochelin or its mirror image enantio-pyochelin, since the two are made by the same set of genes and differ only in stereochemistry.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); pyochelin is not fluorescent, so in a pyoverdine producer it is seen by HPLC-MS or in a pyoverdine-negative background, and the stereochemistry needs chiral HPLC (Youard et al. 2007, doi:10.1074/jbc.m707039200).

column8: A call means an achromobactin-type citrate siderophore cluster is present, and since the same enzyme families also build staphyloferrin B and vibrioferrin, the identity rests on the whole cluster rather than on any one gene.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); achromobactin is not fluorescent, so in a pyoverdine producer it is detected in a pyoverdine-negative background or by HPLC-MS, as was done when the pathway was reconstituted (Berti & Thomas 2009, doi:10.1128/JB.00457-09).

column8: A call means an alcaligin cluster is present, not that the strain is one of the Bordetella or Achromobacter species in which alcaligin was described, nor that the siderophore is made under the conditions you grow the strain in.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); alcaligin is a hydroxamate, so it also gives a positive Csaky-type test, and it is identified by HPLC-MS.

column8: A call means a putrescine-based dihydroxamate cluster is present; putrebactin, bisucaberin and avaroferrin are made by these same three enzymes from whichever diamine the cell supplies, so the rule does not fix which macrocycle the strain closes.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); the macrocycle itself is identified by HPLC-MS, as in the work that assigned the cyclodimerisation step to PubC and the work that showed one enzyme makes all three macrocycles (Kadi et al. 2008, doi:10.1021/ja8027263; Rutschlin et al. 2017, doi:10.1016/j.chembiol.2017.03.017).
column10: Kadi et al. 2008, doi:10.1021/ja8027263; Li et al. 2016, doi:10.1021/acschembio.6b00629; Rutschlin et al. 2017, doi:10.1016/j.chembiol.2017.03.017

column8: A call means a citrate-hydroxamate cluster of this type is present and says nothing about symbiosis; it also cannot separate rhizobactin 1021 from schizokinen, the same six enzymes being credited with both.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); the siderophore is identified by HPLC-MS, and the loss of siderophore production in a cluster mutant is the genetic confirmation (Lynch et al. 2001, doi:10.1128/jb.183.8.2576-2585.2001).

column8: A call means a mycobactin-type salicylate-capped cluster is present; it does not distinguish the lipid-tailed cell-associated mycobactin from the secreted carboxymycobactin, and in an isolate under test it is a flag about which genus you are holding rather than a product claim.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); mycobactins are extracted into organic solvent and identified by HPLC-MS, and iron-limited growth of a cluster mutant is the genetic confirmation.

column8: A call means the pseudomonine cluster is present, not that the strain releases the free salicylate that the same pathway can also produce, which is a separate question answered by measuring salicylate itself.
column9: CAS agar (Schwyn & Neilands 1987, doi:10.1016/0003-2697(87)90612-9); pseudomonine is detected by HPLC and identified by mass spectrometry, the salicylate released by the same pathway is measured colorimetrically as its ferric complex, and the loss of salicylate in a pmsB mutant is the genetic confirmation (Mercado-Blanco et al. 2001, doi:10.1128/jb.183.6.1909-1920.2001).
column10: Mercado-Blanco et al. 2001, doi:10.1128/jb.183.6.1909-1920.2001; Sattely & Walsh 2008, doi:10.1021/ja804499r

column2: ACC deaminase (lowers the plant's stress ethylene)
column8: A call does not prove ACC deaminase activity, because D-cysteine desulfhydrases share the fold and differ from it at only two active-site residues.
column9: Growth on ACC as the sole nitrogen source and the alpha-ketobutyrate assay of ACC deaminase activity (Penrose & Glick 2003, doi:10.1034/j.1399-3054.2003.00086.x)
column10: Glick 2014, doi:10.1016/j.micres.2013.09.009; Todorovic & Glick 2008, doi:10.1007/s00425-008-0820-3; Nascimento et al. 2014, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0099168; Prigent-Combaret et al. 2008, doi:10.1111/j.1574-6941.2008.00474.x

column8: A call shows the two genes of the indole-3-acetamide route, not how much IAA the strain makes, which also depends on tryptophan supplied by the root.
column9: Salkowski colorimetric test of supernatant from cultures given tryptophan (Gordon & Weber 1951, doi:10.1104/pp.26.1.192), confirmed by HPLC or LC-MS because the reagent also reacts with other indoles (Glickmann & Dessaux 1995, doi:10.1128/aem.61.2.793-796.1995)

column8: Bakta's names and EcoFoldDB do not separate indole-3-pyruvate decarboxylase from related 2-keto-acid decarboxylases that may prefer phenylpyruvate or other keto acids, so a call marks a candidate for this route, not proof of IAA synthesis.
column9: Salkowski colorimetric test of supernatant from cultures given tryptophan (Gordon & Weber 1951, doi:10.1104/pp.26.1.192), confirmed by HPLC or LC-MS because the reagent also reacts with other indoles (Glickmann & Dessaux 1995, doi:10.1128/aem.61.2.793-796.1995)

column8: Nitrilases accept many nitriles and the substrate indole-3-acetonitrile comes mainly from plants of the cabbage family, so a call is a weak lead, not evidence of IAA production.
column9: Cell extract incubated with indole-3-acetonitrile, with IAA and indole-3-acetamide measured by HPLC: IAA without indole-3-acetamide points to a nitrilase, indole-3-acetamide to the nitrile hydratase and amidase route (Kobayashi et al. 1993, doi:10.1073/pnas.90.1.247; Kobayashi et al. 1995, doi:10.1073/pnas.92.3.714)

column8: A call means the strain can make the precursor GA9, not bioactive GA4, which needs cyp115; most rhizobia lack cyp115 and their GA9 is activated by the host inside the nodule.
column9: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS of GA9 and GA4 in culture or nodule extracts, the analysis used to define the operon products (Nett et al. 2017, doi:10.1038/nchembio.2232)
column10: Nett et al. 2017, doi:10.1038/nchembio.2232; Nett et al. 2017, doi:10.1021/acschembio.6b01038; Nett et al. 2020, doi:10.1128/mSphere.00292-20; Nett et al. 2022, doi:10.1038/s41396-022-01236-5; Morrone et al. 2009, doi:10.1016/j.febslet.2008.12.052

column2: Cytokinin synthesis by adenylate isopentenyltransferase (low confidence)
column8: A call marks the dedicated cytokinin synthase of gall-forming bacteria, not plant benefit, and strains without it can still release cytokinin from tRNA turnover.
column9: Cytokinins in culture filtrate after immunoaffinity purification, by HPLC with radioimmunoassay (Koenig et al. 2002, doi:10.1128/JB.184.7.1832-1842.2002) or by UPLC-MS/MS (Novák et al. 2008, doi:10.1016/j.phytochem.2008.04.022)

column8: Bacterial glutamate decarboxylase mainly serves acid resistance, so a call shows the capacity to make GABA at low pH, not that the strain releases GABA at the root.
column9: GABA in supernatant of cultures grown with glutamate at low pH, measured by the enzymatic GABase microplate assay (Tsukatani et al. 2005, doi:10.1016/j.aca.2005.03.056) or by HPLC
column10: Feehily & Karatzas 2013, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2672.2012.05434.x; Capitani et al. 2003, doi:10.1093/emboj/cdg403

column8: Most bacteria make putrescine for their own use, so a call has little power to tell strains apart and does not mean putrescine reaches the plant.
column9: HPLC of benzoylated polyamines in cells and culture supernatant (Flores & Galston 1982, doi:10.1104/pp.69.3.701)

column8: Most bacteria make spermidine for their own use, so a call has little power to tell strains apart and does not mean spermidine reaches the plant.
column9: HPLC of benzoylated polyamines in cells and culture supernatant (Flores & Galston 1982, doi:10.1104/pp.69.3.701), as used for a spermidine-secreting Bacillus (Xie et al. 2014, doi:10.1094/MPMI-01-14-0010-R)

column8: A call means the strain can make ectoine to protect itself against salt and drying, not that it protects the plant.
column9: HPLC of ectoine in cells grown in medium with added NaCl (Kuhlmann & Bremer 2002, doi:10.1128/AEM.68.2.772-783.2002)

column8: The betA+betB and codA routes only convert choline taken up from outside, and the same enzymes can serve choline breakdown instead: Arthrobacter pascens uses its choline oxidase to grow on choline and glycine betaine, not to accumulate them (Rozwadowski et al. 1991). Where glycine betaine is accumulated it protects the strain against salt, not the plant, and the genes are common enough that a call says little to rank strains.
column9: Growth at high salinity in minimal medium with and without choline (Boch et al. 1996, doi:10.1128/jb.178.17.5121-5129.1996), with glycine betaine confirmed in cell extracts by HPLC or NMR

column8: Trehalose genes are common, so a call shows capacity, not that the strain accumulates trehalose or helps the plant under drought.
column9: Trehalose accumulation in cells grown at high osmolarity, compared with growth (Freeman et al. 2010, doi:10.1111/j.1462-2920.2010.02171.x)

column8: A call is not proof that the strain degrades benzoate or any pollutant: benzoate dioxygenase is one of a family of look-alike ring-hydroxylating enzymes (for toluate, 2-halobenzoate and anthranilate, among others), so the substrate is a lead to test.
column9: Growth on benzoate as the sole carbon source; in extracts of benzoate-grown cells, the step that turns the benzoate cis-diol into catechol is followed as NADH formation (Reiner 1971, doi:10.1128/jb.108.1.89-94.1971)

column8: A call does not say which aromatic compound supplies the catechol (benzoate, phenol, aniline or plant phenolics, for example) or that the strain degrades any named pollutant; it shows the genes that open catechol and route it towards the TCA cycle.
column9: Catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (pyrocatechase) activity, measured as catechol oxygenation, in extracts of cells grown on benzoate (Dorn & Knackmuss 1978, doi:10.1042/bj1740073)
column10: Harwood & Parales 1996, doi:10.1146/annurev.micro.50.1.553; Feist & Hegeman 1969, doi:10.1128/jb.100.2.869-877.1969

column8: A call does not say which aromatic compound is broken down: the ring-cleavage enzyme is one of several look-alike extradiol dioxygenases and also accepts methylcatechols, and the lower enzymes are shared with the breakdown of phenylpropionate, biphenyl, tryptophan (via 2-aminomuconate) and protocatechuate (2,3-cleavage).
column9: Catechol spray test: colonies with catechol 2,3-dioxygenase turn yellow within seconds as they form 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde (Zukowski et al. 1983, doi:10.1073/pnas.80.4.1101); the lower-pathway enzymes can then be assayed in cell extracts (Shingler et al. 1992, doi:10.1128/jb.174.3.711-724.1992)

column8: A call does not mean the strain degrades a named pollutant: protocatechuate is the common exit for 4-hydroxybenzoate and many plant phenolics, and this branch is widespread in soil bacteria.
column9: Growth on 4-hydroxybenzoate or protocatechuate as the sole carbon source, with protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase activity as characterised for the purified Pseudomonas putida enzyme (Bull & Ballou 1981, doi:10.1016/s0021-9258(18)42947-x)
column10: Doten et al. 1987, doi:10.1128/jb.169.7.3168-3174.1987; Harwood & Parales 1996, doi:10.1146/annurev.micro.50.1.553

column8: A call does not mean the strain degrades lignin itself: this route handles small lignin-derived aromatics such as vanillate and syringate through protocatechuate, and its later enzymes are shared with gallate breakdown.
column9: Protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase activity, which needs both the LigA and LigB subunits (Noda et al. 1990, doi:10.1128/jb.172.5.2704-2709.1990), and growth on vanillate or syringate, which needs the last enzyme LigK (Hara et al. 2003, doi:10.1128/JB.185.1.41-50.2003)

column2: Phenol hydroxylation to catechol (multicomponent phenol hydroxylase)
column8: A call means the strain carries the multicomponent phenol hydroxylase, not that it grows on phenol: the catechol still has to be ring-cleaved, and the enzyme has a broad substrate range, so which substituted phenols and cresols are attacked has to be tested. The single-component (PheA/TbuD type) and two-component (PheA1/PheA2 type) flavoprotein hydroxylases are not called, so a strain that is not called may still hydroxylate phenol.
column9: Growth on phenol as the sole carbon source, and phenol-stimulated oxygen uptake in cell extracts, which needs NAD(P)H and added Fe2+ (Powlowski & Shingler 1990, doi:10.1128/jb.172.12.6834-6840.1990)

column8: A call means the strain carries a naphthalene-type ring-hydroxylating system with the steps that follow it, not that naphthalene is mineralised, because the salicylate still has to be degraded by a separate set of genes, and not that naphthalene is the real substrate, because the closest relatives of these enzymes attack other polycyclic and nitro-aromatic compounds.
column9: Growth on naphthalene as the sole carbon source, with the ring-cleavage products and salicylate identified as the end point of the upper pathway (Eaton & Chapman 1992, doi:10.1128/jb.174.23.7542-7554.1992); solid, water-insoluble substrates such as naphthalene are screened on agar by spraying an ethereal solution over the colonies and looking for clearing zones (Kiyohara et al. 1982, doi:10.1128/aem.43.2.454-457.1982); the indigo test on indole-fed cells shows aromatic ring oxidation but is not substrate-specific (Ensley et al. 1983, doi:10.1126/science.6353574)

column8: A call means the strain has a biphenyl-type dioxygenase pathway, not that it degrades any particular PCB congener: a few amino acids in the large subunit decide which congeners are attacked, and that has to be tested.
column9: Growth on biphenyl as the sole carbon source with the ring-fission product 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-phenylhexa-2,4-dienoate accumulating from 2,3-dihydroxybiphenyl (Catelani et al. 1973, doi:10.1042/bj1341063), then congener-specific PCB depletion measured by gas chromatography against a defined congener mixture (Bedard et al. 1986, doi:10.1128/aem.51.4.761-768.1986)

column2: Aerobic toluene ring hydroxylation by a four-component soluble diiron monooxygenase (toluene-4-monooxygenase type)
column8: A call means the strain carries a soluble diiron monooxygenase of the toluene-4-monooxygenase type, not which ring position it attacks nor which substrate it prefers: the same family oxidises benzene, o-xylene and trichloroethene, and the family name does not fix the position, since the toluene-3-monooxygenase member is itself mainly para-hydroxylating (Fishman et al. 2004). Toluene is also attacked by routes this rule does not cover, the toluene dioxygenase route and the toluene ortho-monooxygenase, and its methyl side chain by the TOL-type enzyme of the xylene_methyl_monooxygenase rule. A strain that is not called may therefore still use toluene.
column9: Growth on toluene as the sole carbon source, with the enzyme reconstituted from toluene-grown cells oxidising toluene to p-cresol as the first product (Whited & Gibson 1991, doi:10.1128/jb.173.9.3010-3016.1991); the route on through p-hydroxybenzaldehyde and 4-hydroxybenzoate to protocatechuate is followed in cell-free preparations of the same cells (Whited & Gibson 1991, doi:10.1128/jb.173.9.3017-3020.1991)

column2: Anaerobic toluene degradation by fumarate addition
column5: bssB | bssC | bbsA | bbsB | bbsC | bbsD | badA | bcrA | bamB
column8: A call means the strain carries the fumarate-addition route for a methylated aromatic ring, not that it was shown to grow on toluene without oxygen, and the same gene names also cover the closely related route for p-cresol.
column9: Anoxic growth on toluene, with nitrate as electron acceptor in the denitrifiers or sulfate in the sulfate reducers, which oxidise toluene completely to CO2 and need it supplied in a carrier phase because it is toxic above about 0.5 mM (Rabus et al. 1993, doi:10.1128/aem.59.5.1444-1451.1993); the diagnostic activity is fumarate-dependent benzylsuccinate formation in cell-free extracts, with nitrate needed for the further oxidation to benzoyl-CoA (Biegert et al. 1996, doi:10.1111/j.1432-1033.1996.0661w.x); and the signature metabolite is the (R) isomer, because the CoA-transferase of the pathway forms exclusively 2-(R)-benzylsuccinyl-CoA (Leutwein & Heider 2001, doi:10.1128/JB.183.14.4288-4295.2001)

column2: Xylene and toluene methyl-group oxidation, the first step of the TOL upper pathway
column8: A call means the strain carries the TOL-type methyl-monooxygenase that oxidises the side chain of toluene and the xylenes to the corresponding benzyl alcohol, not that it reaches toluate or completes the pathway, and not that every xylene isomer is attacked.
column9: Growth on m- or p-xylene as the sole carbon source, with the methyl group oxidised through the corresponding benzyl alcohol and aldehyde to the toluate (Worsey & Williams 1975, doi:10.1128/jb.124.1.7-13.1975); which isomers the oxygenase itself attacks is settled by substrate-range tests on the upper pathway (Abril et al. 1989, doi:10.1128/jb.171.12.6782-6790.1989)

column2: Phenylacetate degradation by the aerobic phenylacetyl-CoA (paa) pathway
column5: paaZ | paaN | paaD | paaF | paaG | paaH | paaJ
column8: A call means the strain can probably break down phenylacetate itself, not that it degrades styrene, ethylbenzene or other pollutants, which need their own upstream genes to reach phenylacetate, and the pathway is common, found in about one in six sequenced bacteria.
column9: Growth on phenylacetate as the sole carbon source; the ring-epoxidation step can be measured in vitro as phenylacetyl-CoA- and oxygen-dependent NADPH consumption (Teufel et al. 2010, doi:10.1073/pnas.1005399107)

column2: Phthalate degradation to protocatechuate (aerobic, by phthalate 4,5- or 3,4-dioxygenase)
column5: phtB | phtAd | pcaG | pcaH | ligA | ligB
column8: A call is a lead from gene names and gene order, not proof of phthalate degradation, because ring-hydroxylating dioxygenases for different aromatic acids look alike, and it says nothing about phthalate esters (the plasticisers), which must first be split by an esterase.
column9: Growth on phthalate as the sole carbon source and oxidation of phthalate by phthalate-grown cells, with growth on dibutyl phthalate as a separate test of ester hydrolysis (Eaton & Ribbons 1982, doi:10.1128/jb.151.1.48-57.1982)

column8: A call is a lead from gene names and gene order, not proof of terephthalate degradation, because ring-hydroxylating dioxygenases for different aromatic acids look alike, and it says nothing about PET plastic itself, which must first be broken down to terephthalate by a polyester hydrolase.
column9: Growth on terephthalate as the sole carbon source, with terephthalate consumption and protocatechuate formation followed by HPLC (Sasoh et al. 2006, doi:10.1128/AEM.72.3.1825-1832.2006)

column8: A call means the strain can break the aromatic ring of benzoyl-CoA without oxygen, the step most anaerobic aromatic degradation passes through, not that it degrades a named pollutant, and the same reductase also reduces methyl- and chlorine-substituted benzoyl-CoA, so the genes do not name the substrate.
column9: Anoxic growth on benzoate with nitrate, sulfate or Fe(III), plus benzoyl-CoA reductase activity in cell extracts: the MgATP-dependent spectrophotometric assay for the class I enzyme (Boll & Fuchs 1995, doi:10.1111/j.1432-1033.1995.921_a.x), or, for the tungsten class II enzyme, the reverse reaction from cyclohexa-1,5-diene-1-carbonyl-CoA (Kung et al. 2009, doi:10.1073/pnas.0905073106)

column2: Nitrate reduction to nitrite (respiratory Nar or periplasmic Nap)
column8: A call means the strain can reduce nitrate to nitrite, not that it denitrifies; in nitrite-oxidising bacteria the same NarG/NarH-type proteins (shared KEGG K00370/K00371) work as nitrite oxidoreductase instead.
column9: Nitrite accumulation from nitrate in anoxic nitrate broth, measured with the Griess reaction (Miranda et al. 2001, doi:10.1006/niox.2000.0319).

column2: Nitrite reduction to nitric oxide (denitrification step)
column8: A call marks one denitrification step only: many nirK or nirS carriers lack the later steps and release NO or N2O, and the genes do not guarantee the phenotype.
column9: N2O accumulation from nitrite in anoxic culture with acetylene, which blocks N2O reduction, measured by gas chromatography (Yoshinari & Knowles 1976, doi:10.1016/0006-291X(76)90932-3), or full NO, N2O and N2 gas kinetics (Lycus et al. 2017, doi:10.1038/ismej.2017.82).

column2: Nitric oxide reduction to nitrous oxide (denitrification step)
column8: NO reductases also detoxify NO in bacteria that do not denitrify, so a call does not mean the strain denitrifies or releases N2O.
column9: NO consumption and N2O production in anoxic culture with nitrite, followed by gas kinetics (Lycus et al. 2017, doi:10.1038/ismej.2017.82).

column2: Nitrous oxide reduction to N2 (N2O sink)
column8: A call means the strain may consume N2O; it says nothing about the earlier denitrification steps, and many nosZ carriers, especially clade II, lack the genes that make N2O.
column9: N2O consumption under anoxia, which acetylene blocks (Yoshinari & Knowles 1976, doi:10.1016/0006-291X(76)90932-3), or gas kinetics (Lycus et al. 2017, doi:10.1038/ismej.2017.82).
